title: Water treatment process and technologies
summary: The treatment train is the organising idea: each stage removes what the next cannot handle economically, and questions frequently test the ORDER. The two most valuable insights are that sedimentation efficiency depends on surface area and not on depth, and that turbidity must be removed BEFORE disinfection because particles consume chlorine and shield organisms. Learn the rapid/slow sand filter comparison and the break-point chlorination curve, and most of the subchapter is covered.

sections.heading: The treatment train and its logic
sections.body:
**Conventional surface water treatment:**

> **Screening → Aeration → Coagulation → Flocculation → Sedimentation → Filtration → Disinfection → (storage and distribution)**

with **softening, fluoridation, iron and manganese removal or arsenic removal** added where the raw water requires.

**The order is not arbitrary, and questions test it.** Each stage removes a **coarser** fraction than the next, so that no stage is asked to do work the previous one could have done more cheaply:

| Stage | Removes | Why it must come before the next |
|---|---|---|
| **Screening** | **Floating debris, leaves, fish** | Would clog and damage pumps and later units |
| **Aeration** | **Dissolved gases, taste, odour**; oxidises **iron and manganese** | The oxidised iron must then be settled and filtered out |
| **Coagulation / flocculation** | Destabilises and aggregates **colloids** | Colloids are too fine to settle unaided |
| **Sedimentation** | The bulk of **settleable solids and floc** | Removes 80–90% of turbidity cheaply, so the filters are not overloaded |
| **Filtration** | **Fine residual particles** and most pathogens | Turbidity must be low before disinfection |
| **Disinfection** | **Pathogens** | The final barrier |

**The last row is the most important logical link in the subchapter.** Disinfection must come **after** turbidity removal because:

1. **Particles consume chlorine** — the chlorine demand is exerted on suspended and organic matter instead of on the organisms;
2. **Particles shield organisms** — a bacterium adsorbed on a clay particle is physically protected from the disinfectant.

So chlorinating turbid water wastes chlorine **and** fails to disinfect. That is why the standards require turbidity below **5 NTU** (ideally under 1) before disinfection, and why a treatment plant that loses its filters has lost its disinfection too.

**Selecting the train by raw water quality:**

| Raw water | Treatment required |
|---|---|
| **Clear spring or deep groundwater** | **Disinfection only** |
| Groundwater with iron | Aeration, sedimentation, filtration, disinfection |
| **Low turbidity surface water** (< 20 NTU) | **Slow sand filtration + disinfection** |
| Moderate turbidity | Plain sedimentation, rapid sand filtration, disinfection |
| **High turbidity river water** | **Full conventional train** with coagulation |
| Very high turbidity (monsoon flood) | Pre-sedimentation or a **roughing filter** first |

**The Nepali monsoon problem** deserves note: river turbidity rises from a few NTU in the dry season to **hundreds or thousands of NTU** in monsoon flood, which overwhelms a plant designed for average conditions. The usual responses are a **pre-settling tank or roughing filter**, provision to **increase the coagulant dose**, and — where the raw water is impossible — a short **shutdown** with the service reservoir carrying the town. Designing for the annual average turbidity is a genuine and common error.

sections.heading: Screening, aeration and sedimentation
sections.body:
**Screens:**

| Type | Opening | Removes |
|---|---|---|
| **Coarse (bar) screen / trash rack** | **50 – 100 mm** | Logs, branches, large debris |
| **Medium screen** | 20 – 50 mm | — |
| **Fine screen** | **< 20 mm**, often 3–20 mm | Leaves, small solids |
| Microstrainer | 20 – 60 micron | Algae, plankton |

**Aeration** brings water into intimate contact with air and serves several purposes at once: it **removes dissolved CO₂ and H₂S** (reducing corrosivity and odour), **removes taste and odour** compounds, and — most importantly for groundwater — **oxidises iron and manganese**:

> **soluble Fe²⁺ + O₂ → insoluble Fe³⁺ (ferric hydroxide)**

which can then be **settled and filtered out**. That two-step logic — oxidise, then remove the solid — is the whole basis of iron removal, and it is why aeration alone does not solve an iron problem.

Types: **cascade**, **spray**, **tray (multiple tray)**, **diffused air**, and **mechanical (agitation)**.

**Sedimentation** removes settleable solids by gravity.

**Stokes' law** governs the settling of a discrete particle in the laminar range:

> **v_s = g(ρ_s − ρ)d² / (18 μ)**

The **d²** is the crucial term: **halving the particle diameter reduces its settling velocity fourfold**. That is precisely why **colloids will not settle** — a 1 micron clay particle would take days to fall a metre — and therefore why coagulation exists.

**The design principle — the most examined idea in the subchapter:**

> **Surface loading (overflow) rate = Q / A_surface**
> **A particle is removed if its settling velocity exceeds Q/A**

**So sedimentation efficiency depends on the SURFACE AREA, not on the depth.** This follows from ideal settling basin theory and is genuinely counter-intuitive: a shallow wide tank and a deep narrow tank of the same **plan area** remove the same particles, because a particle entering at the surface has proportionately longer to fall in the deeper tank but the critical velocity Q/A is the same.

Depth still matters in practice, for **sludge storage**, to avoid **scour** of settled sludge, and to keep the flow from short-circuiting — but it does not improve the theoretical removal.

The practical consequence is important: **to improve a sedimentation tank, increase its plan area (or add plates/tubes), not its depth.** That is exactly what a **tube settler or plate settler** does — it inserts many inclined surfaces to multiply the effective settling area within the same tank volume, which is why they can uprate an existing plant several fold.

**Typical design values:**

| Parameter | Plain sedimentation | With coagulation (clariflocculator) |
|---|---|---|
| **Surface loading rate** | **20 – 30 m³/m²/day** | **40 – 50 m³/m²/day** |
| **Detention time** | **2 – 4 hours** | **2 – 2.5 hours** |
| Depth | 3 – 4.5 m | 3 – 4.5 m |
| **Horizontal velocity** | **≤ 0.3 m/min** | — |
| Weir loading | ≤ 300 m³/m/day | — |

**Types of tank:** **horizontal flow (rectangular)**, **radial flow (circular)**, **vertical flow (hopper bottom)**, and the **clariflocculator**, which combines flocculation in a central zone with settling in the surrounding annulus — the standard unit in Indian and Nepali practice because it saves land and structure.

**Types of settling** are classified by particle behaviour, and each occurs in a different unit:

| Type | Behaviour | Occurs in |
|---|---|---|
| **Type I — discrete** | Particles settle independently; Stokes' law applies | Grit chamber, plain sedimentation |
| **Type II — flocculent** | Particles **coalesce as they settle**, so velocity **increases** with depth | Primary sedimentation after coagulation |
| **Type III — hindered (zone)** | The mass settles as a blanket with a distinct interface | **Secondary clarifier** in activated sludge |
| Type IV — compression | Sludge consolidates under its own weight | Sludge thickener |

**Type II is why a flocculent suspension does better than Stokes' law predicts** — the particles grow on the way down, so a deeper tank *does* help in that case. It is the one qualification to the surface-area rule.

sections.heading: Coagulation, flocculation and filtration
sections.body:
**Why coagulation is necessary.** Colloidal particles (**1 nanometre to 1 micron**) carry a **negative surface charge**, so they **repel one another** and remain permanently dispersed. They cause the turbidity and colour that will not settle. **Coagulation neutralises that charge** so the particles can approach and stick together.

**The two stages must be kept distinct**, because they need opposite conditions:

| Stage | Purpose | Mixing |
|---|---|---|
| **Coagulation** | **Destabilises** the colloids — chemical | **RAPID, violent mixing** for 30–60 seconds, to disperse the coagulant instantly |
| **Flocculation** | **Grows** the destabilised particles into settleable floc — physical | **SLOW, gentle stirring** for 20–40 minutes; too vigorous and the floc breaks up |

Getting these the wrong way round is a standard examination trap: violent mixing during flocculation **destroys** the floc it is meant to grow.

**Coagulants:**

| Coagulant | Formula | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Alum (aluminium sulphate)** | Al₂(SO₄)₃·18H₂O | **The commonest**; dose 5–30 mg/l; optimum **pH 6.5–8.5** |
| Ferric chloride / ferric sulphate | FeCl₃, Fe₂(SO₄)₃ | Wider pH range, effective in cold water |
| Ferrous sulphate with lime | — | — |
| Sodium aluminate | — | Used with alum |
| **Polyelectrolytes** | Organic polymers | **Coagulant aids** — strengthen the floc, reduce the alum dose |

**Alum requires alkalinity to work:**

> **Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3Ca(HCO₃)₂ → 2Al(OH)₃↓ + 3CaSO₄ + 6CO₂**

The **aluminium hydroxide floc** is the active agent — a gelatinous precipitate that enmeshes and adsorbs the colloids. The reaction **consumes alkalinity and produces CO₂**, so:

- if the natural alkalinity is insufficient, **lime or soda ash must be added**, or the pH falls out of the effective range and coagulation fails;
- the pH **drops** during coagulation, which is why pH is measured after, not before.

**The jar test** determines the optimum dose and pH experimentally — several jars of the raw water are dosed differently, rapid-mixed, slow-mixed and allowed to settle, and the best combination is read off. It must be repeated as the raw water changes, which in Nepal means **through the monsoon**, since the dose for flood turbidity is quite different from the dry-season value.

**Filtration** is the polishing stage and the principal barrier to pathogens.

**Mechanisms**, which is worth knowing because filtration is not simply straining: **mechanical straining** (only for particles larger than the pore), **sedimentation** within the pores, **adsorption** (electrostatic attraction to the grain surfaces — the dominant mechanism), **biological action** (in a slow sand filter), and **flocculation** within the bed.

Because **adsorption dominates**, a filter removes particles **far smaller than its pores** — which is why a sand bed with pores of tens of microns removes bacteria of one micron.

**Rapid versus slow sand filter — the comparison to memorise:**

| | **Rapid sand filter** | **Slow sand filter** |
|---|---|---|
| **Filtration rate** | **100 – 150 m³/m²/day** | **2.5 – 5 m³/m²/day** — about **30–50× slower** |
| Land required | **Small** | **Very large** |
| Pre-treatment | **Coagulation essential** | **None needed** |
| Sand effective size | 0.35 – 0.55 mm | 0.2 – 0.3 mm (finer) |
| Bed depth | 0.6 – 0.75 m | 0.9 – 1.1 m |
| Uniformity coefficient | 1.3 – 1.7 | 1.8 – 2.5 |
| **Cleaning** | **Backwashing**, every 24–48 h | **Scraping** the top 20–30 mm, every 1–3 months |
| **Bacterial removal** | 80 – 90% | **99 – 99.9%** |
| Operator skill | **Skilled**, with power | **Minimal**, no power |
| Suits | **Large towns**, turbid water | **Small rural schemes**, clear water |

**The slow sand filter's superior bacterial removal** comes from the **schmutzdecke** — a biologically active layer of algae, bacteria and protozoa that develops on the surface and consumes organic matter and pathogens. It is why the filter must be **ripened** for a few days after cleaning before the water is fit to supply, and why scraping removes only the top layer rather than replacing the sand.

**Slow sand filtration is the right technology for small Nepali rural schemes** and this is worth stating plainly: it needs **no chemicals, no power, no skilled operator**, and it achieves better bacterial removal than a rapid filter. Its only costs are **land** and a raw water that is not too turbid — and in a hill scheme fed from a spring, both conditions are usually satisfied.

**Rapid sand filter operation:**

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Backwash rate** | **0.3 – 1.0 m³/m²/min** for 5–15 minutes |
| Bed expansion | **20 – 50%** |
| **Backwash water used** | **2 – 5%** of the water filtered |
| Under-drainage | Manifold and laterals, or a false floor with nozzles |
| Gravel support | Graded layers under the sand |
| Air scour | Often used before water backwash, to break the mud balls |

**Negative head and air binding** is the operating problem to understand: as the bed clogs, the head loss through the upper layers grows until the pressure within the bed falls **below atmospheric**. Dissolved air then comes out of solution, forms bubbles, and **blocks the pores** — which sharply reduces the filtration rate and can lift the bed. It is the signal that **backwashing is overdue**, and it is prevented by maintaining sufficient water depth over the bed and backwashing at the proper head loss (typically 2–2.5 m).

**Mud balls** form when backwashing is inadequate: accumulated floc and sand agglomerate into lumps that sink into the bed, reducing its effective area and creating channels through which unfiltered water passes. **Air scour** and occasional **surface wash** prevent them.

**Other filters:** **pressure filter** (in a closed vessel, for small supplies and swimming pools), **dual media** (anthracite over sand — coarse first, so the whole depth is used rather than only the surface), and **roughing filter** (coarse gravel, used as **pre-treatment for very turbid water**, and widely used in Nepal upstream of a slow sand filter).

sections.heading: Disinfection and special treatments
sections.body:
**Disinfection** kills or inactivates pathogens. It is not sterilisation — the aim is to remove disease-causing organisms, not all life.

**Requirements of a good disinfectant**, which is effectively an argument for chlorine: it must be **effective** against the pathogens present, **safe** for consumers, **economical**, **easy to handle and dose**, capable of **measurement**, and — decisively — must leave a **persistent residual** to protect the water in distribution.

**Chlorine chemistry:**

> **Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HOCl + HCl**
> **HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻**

**HOCl (hypochlorous acid) is about 80 times more effective than OCl⁻**, and the equilibrium between them depends on pH:

| pH | Dominant species | Effectiveness |
|---|---|---|
| **Below 7** | **HOCl** | **High** |
| 7.5 | Roughly equal | Moderate |
| **Above 8.5** | **OCl⁻** | **Much lower** |

**So chlorine's effectiveness FALLS as pH rises** — which is why the standards cap pH at 8.5, and why softening with lime (which raises pH) must be followed by pH correction before chlorination.

**Break-point chlorination** — the curve to understand:

1. Chlorine first reacts with **reducing agents** (iron, manganese, H₂S) — no residual appears.
2. It then reacts with **ammonia and organic nitrogen** to form **chloramines** — the **combined residual** rises.
3. At the **break point**, further chlorine **destroys the chloramines** and the residual **falls to a minimum**.
4. Beyond the break point, **free residual chlorine** appears and rises linearly with dose.

> **Free residual chlorine** — the strong, fast-acting disinfectant, and what the standards require
> **Combined residual (chloramine)** — weaker and slower, but **longer-lasting**

**Dosing beyond the break point is therefore necessary** to obtain a free residual, and it is why the chlorine demand of a water must be measured rather than assumed.

**Practical requirements:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Contact time** | **≥ 30 minutes** before the first consumer |
| **Residual at the consumer** | **0.1 – 0.2 mg/l** (up to 0.5 in an outbreak) |
| Optimum pH | Below 8 |
| **CT concept** | Concentration × time — the measure of disinfection achieved |

**Forms of chlorine:** **chlorine gas** (cheapest for large plants, but hazardous), **bleaching powder / calcium hypochlorite** (33% available chlorine; the usual choice for small schemes), **sodium hypochlorite** solution, and **chlorine dioxide** (effective over a wider pH range, no chloramines).

**Types of chlorination**, by point and purpose:

| Type | Where | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-chlorination** | **Before** treatment | Controls algae, aids coagulation, reduces taste |
| **Post-chlorination** | **After** filtration | The main disinfection |
| Double chlorination | Both | High-risk raw water |
| **Super-chlorination + dechlorination** | Heavy dose then remove excess with SO₂ or activated carbon | Badly contaminated water |
| **Break-point chlorination** | To beyond the break point | To obtain a **free** residual |
| **Dechlorination** | — | Removes excess chlorine and its taste |

**Disinfection by-products (DBPs)** are the recognised drawback: chlorine reacts with natural organic matter to form **trihalomethanes (THMs)** and other halogenated compounds, which are suspected carcinogens. The controls are to **remove organic precursors before chlorination** (by coagulation) and to **avoid over-chlorination** — but the risk from DBPs is universally judged **far smaller than the risk from unchlorinated water**, which is why chlorination remains standard.

**Alternative disinfectants:**

| Method | Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **Ozone** | Very powerful; **no taste**; destroys colour and organics; no THMs | **No residual**; generated on site; costly |
| **Ultraviolet** | No chemicals, no by-products, no taste | **No residual**; needs **clear** water; power required |
| **Boiling** | Reliable at household scale | Fuel cost; no residual; recontamination |
| **SODIS** (solar disinfection) | Free; suits households | Slow, weather-dependent, small volumes |
| Iodine, silver | Special uses | Cost, taste |

**Chlorine's decisive advantage over ozone and UV is the persistent RESIDUAL**, which continues to protect the water through the distribution network against recontamination from a leak or a cross-connection. Ozone and UV disinfect only at the point of application, so a piped system using them still needs a chlorine top-up. That single property is why chlorine has not been displaced.

**Special treatments:**

| Problem | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **Hardness** | **Lime-soda** process (chemical precipitation) or **ion exchange / zeolite** softening |
| **Iron and manganese** | **Aeration** to oxidise, then sedimentation and filtration; or greensand filter |
| **Fluoride excess** | **Nalgonda technique** (alum + lime + bleaching powder), activated alumina, bone char |
| **Fluoride deficiency** | Fluoridation |
| **Arsenic** | **Oxidation then coagulation/filtration**, activated alumina, iron-coated sand, reverse osmosis |
| **Taste and odour** | **Activated carbon** (powdered or granular), aeration, chlorination, ozone |
| Colour | Coagulation, activated carbon |
| **Salinity / TDS** | **Reverse osmosis**, electrodialysis, distillation |
| Algae | Copper sulphate dosing, pre-chlorination, covered reservoirs |

**Arsenic removal for the Terai** deserves the final word. The essential step is **oxidation of As(III) to As(V)** first, because As(V) is far more readily adsorbed and co-precipitated. Practical technologies at household and community scale include the **Kanchan arsenic filter** (developed for Nepal, using iron nails to generate ferric hydroxide which adsorbs arsenic, followed by sand filtration), **activated alumina** units, and **iron-coated sand**. But the first response, where it is available, remains the simplest: **switch to a safe source** — a deeper well, a piped supply, or a tested neighbouring well — because a treatment unit that depends on household maintenance will eventually be neglected.

formulas.label: Stokes' law
formulas.note: The d² term is why colloids will not settle — halving the diameter quarters the settling velocity.

formulas.label: Surface loading (overflow) rate
formulas.expression: Q/A_surface — a particle is removed if its settling velocity exceeds it
formulas.note: Sedimentation efficiency depends on SURFACE AREA, not depth. To improve a tank, add plan area or plate settlers.

formulas.label: Sedimentation design values
formulas.expression: plain: 20–30 m³/m²/day, 2–4 h detention ;  with coagulation: 40–50 m³/m²/day, 2–2.5 h
formulas.note: Horizontal velocity ≤ 0.3 m/min to avoid scouring settled sludge.

formulas.label: Alum coagulation reaction
formulas.note: Consumes alkalinity and lowers pH. Add lime or soda ash if natural alkalinity is insufficient.

formulas.label: Mixing regimes
formulas.expression: Coagulation: RAPID mixing 30–60 s.   Flocculation: SLOW gentle stirring 20–40 min.
formulas.note: Violent mixing during flocculation destroys the floc it is meant to grow.

formulas.label: Filtration rates
formulas.expression: rapid sand 100–150 m³/m²/day ;   slow sand 2.5–5 m³/m²/day
formulas.note: Slow sand achieves 99–99.9% bacterial removal via the schmutzdecke, against 80–90% for rapid.

formulas.label: Backwashing a rapid sand filter
formulas.expression: 0.3–1.0 m³/m²/min for 5–15 min, expanding the bed 20–50%; uses 2–5% of the filtered water
formulas.note: Negative head and air binding signal that backwashing is overdue.

formulas.label: Chlorine chemistry and pH
formulas.expression: Cl₂ + H₂O → HOCl + HCl ;   HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻
formulas.note: HOCl is ~80× more effective than OCl⁻, so effectiveness FALLS as pH rises. Cap pH at 8.5.

formulas.label: Disinfection requirements
formulas.expression: contact time ≥ 30 min ;   residual 0.1–0.2 mg/l at the consumer ;   dose beyond the BREAK POINT
formulas.note: Free residual is the effective disinfectant; combined (chloramine) is weaker but longer-lasting.
